articles.title: The Old Command That Looked Brand New
articles.dek: In 1982, a forty-year-old page of company beliefs guided Johnson & Johnson through its darkest week. The apostle John says the oldest command in the church becomes new in the same way.
articles.quote: An old command becomes new again every time someone obeys it when it costs something.
articles.body:
On a Wednesday morning in late September 1982, a twelve-year-old girl in a Chicago suburb woke up with a cold, and her parents gave her a capsule of Extra-Strength Tylenol. Within hours she was gone. Over the next few days six more people in the Chicago area died the same way, each after swallowing capsules that someone had secretly laced with cyanide and put back on store shelves. The country was frightened, and Johnson & Johnson, the company that made Tylenol, faced the kind of week that business schools still study.

James Burke, the chairman, had every reason to keep the damage small. The poisonings were local, the tampering had happened after the bottles left the factory, and Tylenol was one of the most profitable products the company owned. Advisers warned that a national recall would cost a fortune and might finish the brand for good. Burke and his team pulled roughly 31 million bottles from shelves across the United States anyway, at a cost of around $100 million, and told the public plainly to stop using the product until it was safe.

When people later asked how they made the call so quickly, Burke pointed to a single page. In 1943, Robert Wood Johnson, son of one of the founders, had written a short statement of beliefs called the Credo. Its opening line said the company's first responsibility was to the doctors, nurses, patients, mothers and fathers who used its products. For decades those words had been displayed at headquarters, admired and mostly taken for granted. A few years before the crisis, Burke gathered his senior managers and asked them a blunt question: did they actually believe this old document, or should they take it off the wall? After long and sometimes heated arguments, they decided to keep it and to mean it. So when the worst week came, the answer had already been written down almost forty years earlier, and it only had to be obeyed.

Within months Tylenol returned in triple-sealed, tamper-resistant packaging, an innovation the whole industry soon copied, and the brand recovered most of its market share within about a year. Yet what people remember is older and simpler. A forty-year-old sentence suddenly looked brand new, because a group of people finally lived it on the day it was expensive.

Around the end of the first century, an old man was writing to churches he loved in and around Ephesus. Most scholars identify him as John, the disciple who had leaned against Jesus at the Last Supper, now perhaps the last eyewitness still living. His congregations were hurting. A group of teachers had walked out, claiming a superior spiritual knowledge and denying that Jesus was truly the Christ come in the flesh. John describes the split with a pastor's ache: "They went out from us, but they did not really belong to us" (1 John 2:19). The people left behind were confused and wounded, and some were surely wondering whether they had missed a newer, deeper truth.

John answers by reaching for something old. He calls them "dear friends," which in Greek is closer to "beloved ones," and then he says something that sounds almost like a riddle.

"Dear friends, I am not writing you a new command but an old one, which you have had since the beginning. This old command is the message you have heard. Yet I am writing you a new command; its truth is seen in him and in you, because the darkness is passing and the true light is already shining." (1 John 2:7–8)

So which is it, old or new? The command is love, and it was old in the plainest sense. Moses had written "love your neighbor as yourself" (Leviticus 19:18) well over a thousand years earlier, and John's readers had heard it "since the beginning," from the day the gospel first reached them. The departing teachers were selling novelty, and John simply declined to compete with them on those terms.

Then he turns the word over in his hand. Greek has two common words for "new." One, neos, means new in time: recent, young, just arrived. The other, kainos, means new in kind, fresh in quality, something that has never existed in quite this form before. John uses kainos. It is the same word Jesus used on the night he was betrayed: "A new command I give you: Love one another. As I have loved you, so you must love one another" (John 13:34). The command to love was ancient; the measure of it, "as I have loved you," was something the world had never seen until a Man knelt to wash dusty feet and then walked to a cross.

The phrase that unlocks John's riddle is this one: "its truth is seen in him and in you" (1 John 2:8). One way to read it is that a command becomes new each time it takes on flesh. In Jesus it was embodied fully for the first time. And John dares to say it is also seen "in you," in ordinary believers in Ephesus who were forgiving one another and staying together after a painful church split. An old command becomes new again every time someone obeys it when it costs something.

That is what happened in 1982. The Credo had sat on the wall for nearly four decades, and plenty of employees had walked past it without a second look. It became kainos, new in kind, during the week a company chose to lose a hundred million dollars to protect families it would never meet. The words were exactly the same as in 1943. They had simply been seen, at last, in the people who claimed them.

John gives a reason for his confidence: "the darkness is passing and the true light is already shining." The verb for "passing" is in the present tense, describing something already in motion, like night slipping away while the sky over the mountains turns gray and then gold. He is telling a frightened church that history is moving in one direction. "The world and its desires pass away," he writes a few lines later, "but whoever does the will of God lives forever" (1 John 2:17). Every act of love is a small piece of that dawn arriving early.

He is also honest about the alternative: "Anyone who claims to be in the light but hates a brother or sister is still in the darkness" (1 John 2:9). Claiming costs nothing, in the same way a Credo on a wall costs nothing until the day it is tested. For many of us, the command to love sits where that Credo sat, familiar and quietly admired. We have heard "love one another" since Sunday school and could recite it at any wedding. John's gentle pressure is on whether anyone has seen its truth in us lately.

The test usually arrives in an ordinary place. It might be the kapatid at church who said something unkind last month, or the relative whose name makes the family group chat go silent. Love in those places will cost you something, usually your pride or your right to be proven correct. Yet John promises that "anyone who loves their brother and sister lives in the light, and there is nothing in them to make them stumble" (1 John 2:10). The path is lit for the person who walks it in love.

You do not need to go hunting for some newer, more exciting truth in order to grow. The teachers who left Ephesus promised secret knowledge, and John simply told his people, "As for you, see that what you have heard from the beginning remains in you" (1 John 2:24). The deepest spiritual growth often looks like taking the oldest instruction you know and carrying it out today, toward one particular person.

Before tonight, think of one person whom loving would cost you a little, and do one concrete thing for them, whether it is sending the message you have put off or speaking the kind word you have been holding back. Johnson & Johnson still points to its Credo today, and those words still carry weight because people once paid to keep them. Your faith carries weight in the same way. When the old command is lived out in you, the people around you will see light where they expected darkness, and they will catch a glimpse of the One whose love it was first. The darkness is already passing, and today your small act of love can be one more ray of the morning.

articles.title: Wisdom You Can Taste
articles.dek: With a death sentence hanging over every wise man in Babylon, young Daniel answered the executioner gently and then went home to ask his friends to pray. Scripture's word for his tact turns out to be the word for taste.
articles.quote: Tact is love that tastes its words before it serves them.
articles.illustration: Antoinette Tuff talks down a gunman
articles.body:
On the afternoon of August 20, 2013, a bookkeeper named Antoinette Tuff was working at the front desk of an elementary school in Decatur, Georgia, when a young man walked in carrying an assault rifle and hundreds of rounds of ammunition. He fired at police outside, and some eight hundred children were in the building. The 911 recording of what happened next was later played around the world. Tuff did not scream or argue. She spoke to the young man quietly and plainly, the way you would speak to a troubled nephew, and she told him about her own hard year, about a marriage that had ended and a son with disabilities. She told him that everyone goes through something in life and that it was not too late for him. She said she cared about him. Little by little he put down his weapons, emptied his pockets, and lay on the floor to wait for the officers. Not one person was hurt. Asked afterward how she had stayed so calm, Tuff said she had been praying the whole time.

Her steadiness under that kind of pressure has a long ancestor. About twenty-six centuries ago, in the palace of Babylon, a young Jewish exile also found himself face to face with a man who had come to kill, and he too reached for gentle words and for prayer. His story is one of the warmest lessons in human wisdom the Bible offers.

Daniel had been carried off from Jerusalem as a teenager, around 605 BC, when Nebuchadnezzar first besieged the city (Daniel 1:1–6). Chapter 1 shows him already practicing a kind of courteous courage. Rather than defying the palace official over the king's food, he asked permission and proposed a ten-day test, and the text says that "God had caused the official to show favor and compassion to Daniel" (Daniel 1:9). Daniel learned early that faithfulness and gracious manners can travel together.

Chapter 2 raises the stakes to life and death. Nebuchadnezzar is troubled by a dream and demands that his advisers tell him both the dream and its meaning, a test no honest human could pass. When they protest, "this made the king so angry and furious that he ordered the execution of all the wise men of Babylon" (Daniel 2:12). Daniel and his three friends are counted among the wise men, though no one has even asked them. The man sent to carry out the order is Arioch, whose title is literally something like "chief of the butchers." He arrives at Daniel's door with his orders in hand.

"When Arioch, the commander of the king's guard, had gone out to put to death the wise men of Babylon, Daniel spoke to him with wisdom and tact." (Daniel 2:14)

From Daniel 2:4 onward the book is written in Aramaic, the international language of the empire, and the phrase translated "wisdom and tact" is ʿēṭāʾ ûṭəʿēm. The first word means counsel, sound judgment. The second, ṭəʿēm, is the lovely surprise. At its root it is the word for taste. Its Hebrew cousin appears in Psalm 34:8, "Taste and see that the LORD is good." From that basic sense it grew to mean discernment, the ability to sense what fits a moment, the way a good cook knows by tasting when the sinigang needs more sour. Daniel, in other words, tasted his words before he served them.

The detail fits the book beautifully. Chapter 1 is entirely about food: Daniel refusing the royal table and thriving on vegetables and water. Chapter 2 shows that the young man who was careful about what went into his mouth was just as careful about what came out of it. One way to read the two chapters together is that the discipline of the first prepared him for the crisis of the second.

Watch what his tact actually looked like. He asked a question: "Why did the king issue such a harsh decree?" (Daniel 2:15). He did not accuse the executioner or plead hysterically, and he treated Arioch as a person who could explain things. Arioch did explain, and then something remarkable happened. Daniel "went in to the king and asked for time" (Daniel 2:16), the very thing the other advisers had been condemned for seeking (Daniel 2:8). The difference seems to have been the spirit in which he asked. A calm and respectful question had opened a door that panic had slammed shut.

Then Daniel did the second wise thing, which is easy to miss. "Daniel returned to his house and explained the matter to his friends Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah. He urged them to plead for mercy from the God of heaven concerning this mystery" (Daniel 2:17–18). He was the gifted one, the one God had already given understanding of "visions and dreams of all kinds" (Daniel 1:17), and yet he would not carry this alone. He went home and gathered the people he trusted, and together they prayed.

God answered that night, and Daniel's prayer of thanks contains a small shift in pronouns that says a great deal about his heart. "You have given me wisdom and power," he prays, "you have made known to me what we asked of you, you have made known to us the dream of the king" (Daniel 2:23). The revelation came to Daniel, but he insists the asking was shared. In his own telling, the answer belonged to the whole little circle of friends who had knelt with him.

His kindness reached even further. The very next thing he said to Arioch was, "Do not execute the wise men of Babylon" (Daniel 2:24). These were pagan astrologers and sorcerers, the professional rivals who had failed the king. Daniel could have let them fall and let his own success shine brighter. Instead he spent his first breath of good news pleading for their lives.

Scripture echoes this kind of wisdom elsewhere. Proverbs 15:1 says, "A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger." Centuries after Daniel, Paul used the same kitchen picture when he wrote, "Let your conversation be always full of grace, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how to answer everyone" (Colossians 4:6). Speech seasoned with grace is speech that has been tasted first. Tact is love that tastes its words before it serves them.

Most of us will never meet a gunman at the front desk or an executioner at the door. We do meet angry people, though. A supervisor storms out of a meeting with a harsh new rule, a relative at the family reunion says something that cuts, or a customer at the counter raises their voice over something that was never your fault. The pull in those moments is either to fire back or to fold. Daniel shows a third path, and Antoinette Tuff walked it too: stay calm enough to ask a real question, speak to the angry person as a human being, and then go and find your praying friends.

That last step matters as much as the first. Many of us are brave in the moment and lonely afterward, carrying the pressure of a crisis in silence because we do not want to trouble anyone. Daniel had more spiritual gifts than anyone in Babylon, and still his first move was to knock on his friends' doors. If someone you love is facing something hard this week, you could be a Hananiah to them, and if you are the one facing it, you have every right to ask for a Mishael.

Today, before you answer a sharp word, give yourself the few seconds it takes to taste your reply. Ask one honest question before you defend yourself. And then send a message to two or three people you trust and ask them simply to pray with you. The God who gave a young exile wisdom in the middle of the night is still the God who "reveals deep and hidden things" (Daniel 2:22), and he still loves to answer what his friends ask together.

articles.title: The Cells That Watch for Morning
articles.dek: Deep in your eye, a few cells spend the whole night waiting for dawn. Psalm 130 uses one Hebrew word to show what God chooses to watch, and what he lets you watch for instead.
articles.quote: The God who could have watched your every failure has chosen instead to be the morning you watch for.
articles.body:
For most of the twentieth century, scientists believed they understood how the eye senses light. Rods handled dim light, cones handled color, and those two kinds of cells seemed to be the whole story. Then, in the 1990s, a British researcher named Russell Foster found something that did not fit. Mice bred without any working rods or cones, blind by every standard test, still reset their internal body clocks when the lights came on. Something inside those eyes was still watching for the sun.

The answer, pieced together over the following years, was a small group of cells in the retina carrying a light-sensitive protein called melanopsin. In 2002, neuroscientist David Berson and his colleagues showed that these cells respond to light directly. They send their signal to a tiny cluster of neurons sitting just above the place where the optic nerves cross, the cluster that sets the body's master clock. These cells make up only a small fraction of the retina, and they play almost no part in forming pictures of the world. Their work is simpler and more patient. Through the dark hours they wait, and when the first blue light of morning arrives, they tell the whole body that the night is over.

The discovery has carried real hope with it. In 2007, researchers described people who were completely blind whose bodies still responded to daylight, because these watchful cells had survived when the others had failed. The finding has led some doctors to think more carefully about protecting the eyes of blind patients wherever possible. A person who cannot see the sunrise can still, in a quiet and wonderful way, receive it.

Nearly three thousand years ago, an unnamed poet in Israel wrote a song about waiting for the morning. Psalm 130 belongs to a collection called the Songs of Ascents (Psalms 120 to 134), which many scholars believe pilgrims sang as they climbed the roads to Jerusalem for the great feasts. Many of those songs are bright with family, harvest, and the hills around the holy city. This one begins at the bottom of the world: “Out of the depths I cry to you, LORD; Lord, hear my voice” (Psalm 130:1–2).

The Hebrew word for “depths,” ma'amaqqim, usually describes deep water, the kind that closes over a drowning person's head (Psalm 69:2, 14). The writer never tells us what pulled him under. He tells us only what he fears most, which is that God has been keeping count. His plea is short and urgent, “Let your ears be attentive to my cry for mercy” (Psalm 130:2), because he knows his own record and cannot imagine standing before a holy God with it. Then, in two brief lines, he turns his face toward the light.

“If you, LORD, kept a record of sins, Lord, who could stand? But with you there is forgiveness, so that we can, with reverence, serve you.” (Psalm 130:3–4)

The phrase “kept a record” translates a single Hebrew verb, shamar. It means to watch, to guard, to keep a careful eye on something. It is the word used when God places Adam in Eden “to work it and take care of it” (Genesis 2:15), and the word in the beloved blessing, “The LORD bless you and keep you” (Numbers 6:24). The psalmist pictures a God who stands guard over every sin, watching each one through the night so that none slips away. If that were the truth about God, he says, no one could stand.

Two verses later, the same root appears again. “I wait for the Lord more than watchmen wait for the morning, more than watchmen wait for the morning” (Psalm 130:6). The Hebrew word for “watchmen” is shomerim, literally those who shamar. Within a few lines, the psalm moves the watching from God's side to ours. God declines to stand guard over our sins, and so the one who prays is free to become the watchman, standing on the wall in the dark with his eyes fixed on the eastern sky. One way to read the whole psalm is as a quiet exchange of posts. The God who could have watched your every failure has chosen instead to be the morning you watch for.

Watchmen in ancient Israel knew the night intimately. They stood on city walls through the cold hours, listening for raiders and peering into the darkness, and their shift ended only when daylight made the hills visible again. The psalmist repeats his line twice on purpose, the way a weary guard might murmur it to himself near four in the morning. Yet a watchman never wonders whether the morning will come. He waits because he is certain of it, and that is the kind of hope the psalm describes when it says, “in his word I put my hope” (Psalm 130:5).

Verse 4 also carries a surprise about what forgiveness produces. The psalmist says it leads to reverence, “so that we can, with reverence, serve you.” A person excused by a stranger may simply shrug and move on, but a person forgiven by someone who loves them tends to walk more gently afterward, because they have glimpsed what that mercy cost. The Hebrew even includes a definite article, hasselichah, “the forgiveness,” as though the writer has in mind a particular, settled mercy that lives with God and waits for whoever comes to ask.

The rest of Scripture echoes this picture. Paul writes that love “keeps no record of wrongs” (1 Corinthians 13:5), and Martin Luther counted Psalm 130 among his favorite psalms, calling it one of the “Pauline psalms” because it holds the good news of grace so plainly. The song ends on ground the New Testament will later stand on: “with the LORD is unfailing love and with him is full redemption. He himself will redeem Israel from all their sins” (Psalm 130:7–8). The word for unfailing love is hesed, God's loyal covenant love, the love that keeps its promises even when we break ours.

Many of us lie awake in our own ma'amaqqim. Perhaps it is an old sin you still replay at two in the morning, a harsh word spoken to a parent who has since passed away, or a failure no one else knows about. We often keep the record ourselves, standing guard over our mistakes as though letting go of them would be dishonest. Psalm 130 gently invites you to leave that post, because if the holy Lord has chosen to set that record down, you do not need to keep it for him.

Then take up the better watch. Like those small cells in the eye that spend the night ready for the first light, you can turn your heart toward God's morning. Tonight, before you sleep, you might pray verses 3 and 4 over the very thing that troubles you, name it plainly, and leave it in his hands. Tomorrow, when the first light reaches your window or you hear the early tricycles and the neighbor's rooster, let it remind you that the Lord's “compassions never fail. They are new every morning” (Lamentations 3:22–23).

The night may still feel long, and the psalmist never pretends otherwise, which is why he repeats the watchman's line twice. Yet the morning he waits for is as sure as the sunrise those quiet cells keep watching for, and it comes from a God who has laid down the ledger and taken up your hope. Wait for him with your whole being. He is already on his way to you.

articles.title: More Hope for a Fool
articles.dek: Proverbs spends eleven verses laughing at the fool, then points to someone in even worse shape. The surprise is who that person is, and why grace finds it so hard to reach them.
articles.quote: Grace has never had trouble finding fools. It waits at the door of anyone willing to admit they are one.
articles.illustration: Hokusai, the old man mad about drawing
articles.body:
In 1834, an old man in Edo, the city we now call Tokyo, sat down to write a short note for the back of a book of his own woodblock prints. He was Katsushika Hokusai, and he was already famous. A few years earlier he had published The Great Wave off Kanagawa, the curling blue wave with its claw-like foam that still appears on dorm walls, coffee mugs, and phone screens from Manila to Madrid. By any measure he had arrived. Yet the afterword he wrote that year for One Hundred Views of Mount Fuji sounds like a beginner's diary.

"From the age of six I had a mania for drawing the shapes of things," he wrote. He admitted that nothing he had made before seventy was worth much, and that at seventy-three he had finally "learned a little about the real structure of nature." Then he made a cheerful plan: by eighty he hoped to improve, by ninety to grasp the mystery of things, and by a hundred and ten, he said, every dot and line he drew would be alive. In those years he signed some of his work Gakyō Rōjin, "the old man mad about drawing." When he lay dying at eighty-eight, his friends recorded him asking heaven for five more years so that he could become a real painter.

Filipinos know this kind of elder. He is the lolo who has fixed fishing boats for fifty years and still watches the young mechanic's new trick with real curiosity, or the retired teacher who keeps a notebook of new words she learns from her apo. We trust such people deeply, and part of the reason is that they never stopped being teachable. The book of Proverbs has a sharp word for the opposite kind of person, and it lands in a place most readers do not expect.

Proverbs 26 opens with a long, almost comic portrait of the fool. This section belongs to the proverbs of Solomon that, according to Proverbs 25:1, were "compiled by the men of Hezekiah king of Judah," royal scribes some two centuries after Solomon who gathered his sayings for a new generation. In the first twelve verses of chapter 26, the word "fool" appears in nearly every line. The Hebrew word is kesil, and it describes a dull, stubborn person who has heard wisdom many times and simply refuses to let it in. The writer piles up pictures of him the way a cartoonist sketches a caricature.

A proverb in the fool's mouth is "like the useless legs of one who is lame" (Proverbs 26:7), because the words are there but they carry him nowhere. Honoring a fool is "like tying a stone in a sling" (Proverbs 26:8), which defeats the whole purpose of the sling. Wisdom in his hands is "like a thornbush in a drunkard's hand" (Proverbs 26:9), waved around carelessly until someone bleeds. Hiring him is like "an archer who wounds at random" (Proverbs 26:10). Then comes the picture nobody forgets: "As a dog returns to its vomit, so fools repeat their folly" (Proverbs 26:11). By the end of verse 11, the reader is fairly sure the fool sits at the very bottom of the ladder, as hopeless a case as the Bible can describe.

Then verse 12 turns the whole passage around. It does so with a question aimed straight at the reader.

"Do you see a person wise in their own eyes? There is more hope for a fool than for them." (Proverbs 26:12)

After eleven verses of laughing at the fool, the writer points to someone even worse off, and the description is uncomfortably ordinary. The Hebrew phrase is chakam be'enav, "wise in his eyes." The person in view may be bright, experienced, and successful. The trouble lies in where they look for the verdict on themselves, because their own eyes have become the final judge. Proverbs warns about this from its opening chapters: "Do not be wise in your own eyes; fear the LORD and shun evil" (Proverbs 3:7). The prophet Isaiah speaks even more strongly: "Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes and clever in their own sight" (Isaiah 5:21).

Why would the fool have more hope? One way to read it is that the fool still has a door that can open. Shame, failure, a hard season, or a patient friend might finally get through to him, and the whole book of Proverbs is written on the conviction that the untaught can still be taught (Proverbs 1:4). The person who is wise in their own eyes has quietly locked that door from the inside. They hear correction well enough, and then they file it away as someone else's problem. Hokusai, at the height of his fame, kept his door wide open, and that is why he kept growing until the day he died.

This is where Proverbs 26:12 points toward the gospel. Jesus told a story "to some who were confident of their own righteousness and looked down on everyone else" (Luke 18:9). Two men went up to the temple to pray. The Pharisee, a respected religious man, thanked God that he was better than other people and listed his fasting and his tithes. The tax collector, a man his neighbors considered a traitor and a cheat, stood at a distance, beat his breast, and said, "God, have mercy on me, a sinner" (Luke 18:13). Jesus said it was the tax collector who "went home justified before God" (Luke 18:14), meaning he was declared right with God.

The Pharisee is Proverbs 26:12 in sandals. He walked into the very house of mercy and walked out unchanged, because he never asked for any. The tax collector is the fool who finally said so out loud, and that admission became his open door. Jesus said the same thing at Levi's dinner table: "It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick. I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners" (Mark 2:17). Paul echoed it for the clever believers in Corinth: "If any of you think you are wise by the standards of this age, you should become 'fools' so that you may become wise" (1 Corinthians 3:18). Grace has never had trouble finding fools. It waits at the door of anyone willing to admit they are one.

Being wise in our own eyes rarely feels like arrogance from the inside. It feels like being reasonable, and it sounds like "I know my child better than that teacher does," or "I've served in this ministry for twenty years, so I hardly need advice from someone half my age." In Filipino culture, where age and position carry real weight, it can hide behind hiya and pride, making it painfully hard to say "I was wrong" in front of someone younger, someone junior, or the whole family. Many of us have lost years to a mistake we kept repeating, like the dog of verse 11, simply because admitting it felt too costly.

The way back is surprisingly practical. Choose one area of your life where you have been certain for a long time, perhaps a habit, a long-running conflict, or the way you handle money or anger, and bring it to someone who loves you enough to be honest, such as your spouse, an older believer, or a trusted friend from church. Ask them plainly, "What do you see in me here that I might be missing?" When they answer, resist the urge to explain yourself, write down what they said, and take it to God in prayer, asking him to show you whether it is true. That one humble conversation can move you out of verse 12 and back into the place where hope lives.

This is good news, and it should make your heart lighter today. The only qualification for drawing near to God is a heart honest enough to be taught, and the Lord has always been glad to meet people who know they still have much to learn. Hokusai at seventy-three said he had "learned a little," and he went on drawing with fresh delight for fifteen more years. Carry his posture into this day, and carry the tax collector's prayer alongside it: "God, have mercy on me." A heart that can pray that sentence has a great deal of hope.
